title: Grammar: voice, aspect, tense, modality and sentence structure

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Recognise voice, aspect, tense and modality, and analyse word order, sentence type and sentence length as choices with effects.

blocks.heading: Voice, aspect, tense and modality
blocks.text: Grammatical voice is whether a clause is active, with the doer as subject, or passive, with the thing acted on as subject; it is not the same as a writer’s voice, which is the sense of a particular person speaking. Aspect is how an action is seen in time: progressive presents it as ongoing (is rising), perfect as completed with present relevance (has risen). Tense places an action in time, and the present tense used for past events pulls the reader into the scene as if it were unfolding. Modality is how far a writer commits: modal verbs and adverbs express certainty, possibility or obligation; high modality asserts, low modality leaves room.

blocks.heading: What grammar does
blocks.text: The passive in a sentence can hide or remove the agent, which suits a writer who wants the action without the actor: "mistakes were made" leaves the reader with nowhere to put blame. High modality asserts a writer’s authority, low modality sounds open and advisory, and each earns its effect against the text’s purpose and audience: a doctor writing "this will pass" reassures; one writing "this may pass" has said less, honestly or not. A shift from past to present tense makes events feel immediate, as if the reader were beside them rather than hearing a report: "Then the lights fail. Someone shouts." That is the historic present doing its work.

blocks.heading: Sentence types
blocks.text: A simple sentence is one clause; a compound sentence joins clauses of equal weight; a complex sentence carries one main clause with one or more dependent clauses. A minor sentence is a deliberate fragment without a finite verb — "Not this time." — and is not the same as an accidental fragment, which is an error. Syntax is the order of words in a sentence, and that order decides what the reader meets first; fronting moves an element to the start, so the reader meets it first and gives it focus.

blocks.heading: Worked example: the passive and the agent
blocks.text: Compare two sentences, written for the purpose: "The council repaired the bridge" and "The bridge was repaired." The active sentence names the doer, so the reader knows who to credit; the passive hides the agent, so the repair stands alone, and the reader cannot tell who acted. If the writer of the second sentence works for the council, the passive is doing a job: the action is on record and the actor is not. The analysis says that, which is what a label alone never does.

blocks.heading: Length and order as choices
blocks.text: A short sentence creates emphasis or tension by contrast with the longer sentences around it; a list of three builds weight through its rhythm and its sense of completion. Fronting shifts the reader’s focus to whatever has been moved first: "Down came the rain" makes the rain the news, where "The rain came down" makes the coming the fact. The moves are not decoration: they are how a writer tells the reader where to look.

blocks.heading: Sentence length in action
blocks.text: Watch a paragraph of a report move: "The inspection covered four tanks on Tuesday." A simple sentence opens, and the reader receives one fact at walking pace. "Because the third tank had been drained for repair, the inspector climbed inside, checked the seams and photographed what he found." A complex sentence follows, and the reader receives cause, action and evidence in one breath, which is the report telling them the fact is anchored. "Nothing." A minor sentence closes the sequence, and its brevity against the sentences around it performs the emptiness the inspector found. Three types, three effects: the analysis is that easy to find and that easy to miss by labelling.

blocks.heading: Labels are not analysis
blocks.text: The error to avoid is labelling sentences simple, compound or complex and saying nothing about what the structure does. After the label, ask what the structure makes this reader notice or feel at that point: a complex sentence at the moment of a flood carries the water’s cause and its consequence in one breath, which is the point. If the label is deleted and nothing about meaning or effect is left, nothing was analysed.
